text: Priya had ten minutes to reach the dentist and no place to park. 'Get me a parking spot near Elm Street,' she said to her phone, 'but not the garage, I do not want to pay the new price.' The assistant understood that she wanted a spot on the street and not the garage. It found a free space one block away, in front of a shop with a blue blind over the door, and it showed her the way. Priya parked in two minutes. Then she said, 'Tell me when my time runs out.' The assistant set a timer for the two hours the sign allowed and promised to speak up ten minutes before the end.

name: birthday_lookup
does: Finds a person's birthday in the contacts and can send an hourly reminder on that day until you say stop.
inputs: the person's name
people say:
- When does Anna turn forty?
- Whose birthday is coming up this week?
- Dim the lights and tell me what day my brother was born, I am making a playlist for him
- Nag me every hour on Sam's birthday so I do not forget the cake
- Do I know anyone who was born in May?

Person: I am not good with this stuff. Can you explain how I see my front door when I am out?
Assistant: Yes. Do you want to watch it live, or get a message when someone comes?
Person: A message. I do not want to look at it all day.
Assistant: Okay. Which door should I watch, the front or the back?
Person: The front one. I am going to my sister's for a meal.
Assistant: Done. The front camera will send a message to your phone if it sees anyone move.
Person: Lovely. My favourite part is that I do not have to press anything.
Assistant: Right, you just ask me. Would you like the alarm on too?
Person: No, thank you. Just the camera.

Marco the cook was making soup for forty guests when his dad called to say he was coming early. 'Make the kitchen lights twice as bright,' Marco told the assistant, 'I can barely see my knife.' The assistant raised the ceiling lights to full. A little later Marco wanted a calm mood for the dining room. 'Show me the colours,' he said, and he scrolled through the list on his tablet. 'What is the least bright blue you have?' The assistant picked the dimmest blue setting for the bulbs and turned the dining room lights to that. Marco smiled and went back to his soup.

Lena owned a toy shop, and the lantern festival was only days away. 'Add paper lanterns to my list and tell me if Friday will be stormy,' she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted two things: put paper lanterns on the shopping list, and check the weather for Friday. It added the lanterns and then said Friday would be stormy, with strong wind in the afternoon. Lena had planned to hang the lanterns in the yard outside the shop. She touched the screen and asked the assistant to move the plan to Saturday instead. The assistant changed her reminder to Saturday morning.

Ben was lying in bed. His mum had told him about a toy sale on Saturday, so he said to the speaker, 'Wake me up at six so we can go to the sale.' The speaker set an alarm for six. Then Ben yawned. 'No, not six, the shop opens at nine. Make it eight.' The assistant understood that he had fixed the time, and it changed the alarm to eight. Ben wanted his room to look neat in the morning, so he asked the assistant to remind him to put his shoes away. Then he asked it to raise the volume of the lullaby a little. The assistant did, and Ben fell asleep.

A packing list is a short note of what to take on a camping trip, so nothing important stays at home. People keep it on their phone and change it before each trip, saying things like 'add a stove so we can cook' or 'remove the big tent, we are only two'. Families who camp every month usually reuse the same list and change only a few lines. Many also check the weather in the hills the night before, asking 'will it be cold up there on Saturday?' A photo of the trail map is useful too, because the phone may have no signal on the trail.

Omar owned a bakery and drove a small van. Before the morning rush he said to his car, 'How much petrol do I have?' The assistant answered that the tank was less than a quarter full, about eleven litres. Omar's mouth went dry. He had a single stop to make before opening, but he did not want to run out. 'Find me the closest station,' he said, 'and I prefer one on my way to the shop.' The assistant found a station half a mile ahead on the same road and started the directions. Omar filled the tank and reached the bakery with time to spare.

Nadia ran a tiny bookshop two kilometers from the bus stop. At closing time her phone showed that someone had asked to see her shop photos. She typed fast, all in lowercase: cancel the sharing on the black tablet and lcok my phone. The assistant found the black tablet in her list of devices and stopped it from sharing the photo folder. Then it locked her phone, so it needed a passcode to open. It told her that nobody else could see the folder now. Nadia put the phone in her bag and turned off the lights.

Jin woke up late and rubbed both eyes. 'When is the rent due?' Jin asked the speaker, still half asleep. 'No, not the rent, I mean the internet bill.' The assistant understood the correction and said the internet bill was due on the twentieth. That was close, only two days away, and it was thirty dollars. Outside, a neighbour began to shout about the gate, because a delivery man had left it open. Jin said, 'Pay it today.' The assistant answered that it would pay the thirty dollars that afternoon and send a message afterwards. Jin pulled the blanket back up.
